drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here is your opening item. A recruiter has two hundred applications
drills.answer_line: SAM: It cannot guarantee the outcome
drills.stem: A recruiter wants Claude to rank 200 applications and automatically reject the bottom half. Hiring policy requires decisions against the published criteria. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Go ahead: Claude ranks well and it saves days
options.B: Go ahead, but instruct Claude to be fair and ignore gender, age and ethnicity
options.C: Claude summarises against published criteria; recruiter makes every decision; check the shortlist for bias patterns
options.D: Do not use Claude anywhere in hiring

drills.why: An instruction cannot guarantee the outcome and nobody would know if it failed. A person owns each decision, and checking the set catches bias no single summary shows.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Four statements, each with a dropdown
drills.prompt: For each, choose: appropriate; appropriate with human review before it goes out; or not appropriate. 1. Brainstorming names for an internal newsletter. 2. Summarising a patient's history for a clinician. 3. Writing five-star customer reviews for the product page. 4. Drafting a reply to a customer charged twice.
drills.answer: 1. Appropriate. 2. With review, by the clinician. 3. Not appropriate: deceptive. 4. With review: it goes to a customer and admits or disputes a billing error.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A logistics analyst wants Claude to find patterns
drills.answer_line: SAM: C is right. D is a comfort control
drills.stem: A logistics analyst wants patterns in late deliveries by region and time slot. The export holds customer names, mobile numbers and addresses, plus region, time slot and minutes late. Policy restricts sharing customer personal data. Which two steps are most appropriate?

options.A: Replace customer names with reference codes, so a pattern can be traced back internally
options.B: Upload to a personal account to skip a week-long approval
options.C: Remove mobile numbers, addresses and other columns the analysis does not need
options.D: Use an incognito chat so the data is not kept
options.E: Upload as is and ask Claude to delete it afterwards

drills.why: Only the data the task needs. Incognito governs memory and history, not what policy allows; an instruction to delete is not a control.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A marketing coordinator realises she pasted
drills.answer_line: SAM: C. Deleting the chat takes it off her list
drills.stem: A marketing coordinator realises she pasted a customer list with names and emails into a chat in the company workspace, against the policy for that data. What is the best next action?

options.A: Delete the chat and carry on
options.B: Ask Claude to forget the list
options.C: Stop using the data and report it through the policy's incident process
options.D: Do nothing, since the workspace is approved

drills.why: Deleting the chat does not settle what happened; data-protection owners decide what follows. An approved tool is not an approved use.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A company's I T team has built a customer chat assistant
drills.answer_line: SAM: C. Presenting an A I as a named human
drills.stem: IT has built a customer chat assistant on Claude. Marketing wants it to introduce itself as Sarah from the support team, because customers seem to prefer people. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Agree, since customer satisfaction is the goal
options.B: Agree, and mention AI use in the terms of service
options.C: It says clearly it is an AI and offers a route to a person; raise the request through governance

drills.why: Presenting an AI as a named human misleads the customer; disclosure is the control. B hides it; D abandons a working assistant.

drills.question_line: SAM: Your turn first. Pause and name the four tasks we covered, and the distractor each one invites. [pause]
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Use cases: abandoning the task.
drills.prompt: Name the four tasks we covered, and the distractor each one invites.
drills.answer: Use cases: abandoning the task. Data: uploading as is, or trusting a setting. Policy: treating silence as permission. Ethics: an instruction standing in for a check, or hiding the AI.

In this episode: Sort a use case by its risk
Strip data to what the task needs
What policy decides, and what to do when it is silent
Bias, deception, and decisions nobody owns
Cold open: two hundred applicants: 4 tasks: use cases, data, policy, ethics
3 distractor families: as if nothing were sensitive, abandon, model promise
Appropriate and inappropriate use: Ask: what if it's wrong, and to whom?
Higher stakes: decisions about people, public output
Qualified means able to catch that field's errors
Deceptive or harmful uses are out whatever the case
"Do not use" is a distractor family
Data sensitivity, regulation and privacy: Classes: public, internal, confidential, regulated personal
Minimum necessary: drop, code or aggregate
The approved workspace, not a personal account
Instructions to the model are not policy controls
Incognito: out of memory and history, not out of governance
Organisational AI policy: Policy decides tools, data, review, disclosure, reporting
Admins configure; you work inside it
Low-stakes internal work vs restricted data, customers, people
Something went wrong: the policy's reporting route
Ethics: Performance-review summaries: the bias was in the input
Not every draft needs a bias check
Disclose when the reader would act differently
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: C, summaries against criteria, the recruiter decides, check the pattern
An instruction to be fair cannot guarantee the outcome
Nobody would know if the instruction failed
A: an automatic cut that nobody owns; D: abandons the task
Five to remember: Judge by what happens if it's wrong; deceptive uses are out
Don't abandon a task a control can make safe
Minimum data in the approved workspace; instructions and incognito aren't controls
Silence is not permission; report incidents by the policy's route
Bias across the set, disclose AI, a person owns every output
Recap: the exam tells: Automatic decision about a person → human back in, check the pattern
"Skip it" or "stop using Claude" → distractor unless prohibited
"Policy restricts" → strip or code fields before upload
"Tell Claude not to keep it" or incognito → comfort control
Policy silent → ask the owner; gone wrong → report it
Reader would believe a human did it → disclose
Each output fine alone → compare the set
